newsitem.title: UK: Crude tanker market steady but pressure zones loom.
newsitem.headline: Crude tanker market steady but pressure zones loom.

text.p: The crude tanker market closed the week relatively steady in quiet business and brokers expected Mideast/Japan VLCC fixtures to come under pressure next week while a question mark hung over rates from West African ports after a number of failures.
Mideast/Japan rates for 250,000 tonners held at W65 through the week but at least two brokers saw lower numbers next week.

"There's a lot of tonnage and not much demand for younger vessels. It's 65 and dropping and I expect the South Koreans to hammer the rates next week and we might see them 2.5 points lower," a broker said.

Galbraith's brokerage said in a weekly report that the last fixture for Mideast/Korea showed signs of weakness with the Argo Daphne for 260,000 tonnes fixed at W59, compared with earlier fixtures in the week at W62.5 for similar tonnage.
"Although these Red Sea loaders are generally fixed at slightly less than those from the AG, this particular deal does represent a slight fall," they said.
Business for ULCCs was virtually non-existent and the list of early tonnage was growing with the next deal out of the Middle East expected to be at lower numbers, they added.

Older vessels languished and Galbraith's said competition among owners was so fierce that India's PTT was able to fix the Doha for 260,000 tonnes loading February 23 loading in the Mideast Gulf for Thailand at W47.5.
The talk of the week was the number of failures from West Africa, which saw a large number of enquiries for VLCCs but the number of deals reported made for a confusing picture.
"So many ships have been put on subs and failed, it has become quite a nightmare for owners to actually know what is real and what is not in this area," Galbraith's said in their report.
Out of 10 vessels on subs, only four were confirmed over the last week, they added.

"The reason is that many of the players are traders who are trying to combine stems with others who are trying to do the same as their competitors. As a result, ships have been held on subs for 24 hours whilst these traders scramble around the market to fill up the space," the report said.

Despite that VLCC rates from the region held at fairly healthy numbers with a couple of older units booked for 260,000 tonners at W67.5 to the U.S. Gulf while one modern ship, the Magdala, managed W70 for a March 3 loading.
Suezmax tonnage out of West Africa was very tight for the rest of the month and only a couple of VLCCs were seen available, which could lead to higher rates next week, Galbraith's said.
Business in the Mediterranean was subdued with Suezmax tonnage fetching W85-W90 depending on the length of trip.
Aframax activity in the Mediterranean fell off and 80,000 vessels fetched an average W127.4 for inter-Med voyages.
The picture for Aframax business in the Caribbean market was depressing, with rates continuing to slump for 70,000 tonners.
"The meltdown continued in the Caribbean, with 70,000 tons Caribs/USAC now trading at around W115 and a typical 76,000 East Coast Mexico/US Gulf as low as W105," Galbraith's said.

"It was only a mere two weeks ago that this market was about 50 worldscale points more -- the reason is simply that business has been less and...as a consequence, oil company re-lets have been competing with the independent owner," the report said.
It added that while Aframax rates in the Far East was holding at W135-W145 for cross-regional business, rates could come under pressure next week.
-- Kate Dourian, London newsroom +44 171 542 7629
